doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c01819.title: Termination-Dependent Surface Fermiology in the Intercalated Altermagnet CoNb4Se8
doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c01819.abstract: Abstract Altermagnets have recently gained attention for hosting symmetry-enforced spin-split bands despite zero net magnetization. Angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (ARPES) offers direct access to their electronic structure. However, the intrinsic surface sensitivity of this technique complicates the identification of the observed features: Surface states can be misinterpreted as the spin-split counterpart of bulk bands. This issue becomes particularly relevant for layered intercalated systems, where micrometer-sized domains with distinct terminations often coexist on a cleaved surface. We discuss this scenario for CoNb4Se8, one of the first established layered altermagnets. Supported by density functional theory calculations, we employ micro-ARPES to probe individual domains and reveal two contrasting surface terminations. We identify Co- and Se-terminated domains with characteristic surface states arising from bulk-surface connectivity of the material. Our work shows that termination-dependent surface contributions are essential for the reliable spectroscopic identification of altermagnetism and for assessing its presence across the family of layered materials.

doi:10.1021/jacs.6c16624.title: Planar Benzene Trianion-Bridged Dilanthanide Complexes Exhibiting Strong Ferromagnetic Exchange via Metal–Radical Covalency
doi:10.1021/jacs.6c16624.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
doi:10.1021/jacs.6c16624.abstract: Abstract The synthesis of molecules exhibiting strong magnetic exchange coupling between contracted lanthanide 4f electrons and a radical spin presents an important challenge relevant to the design of single-molecule magnets and solid-state magnetic materials. Concurrently, the isolation of a planar benzene trianion radical remains an unrealized target. Here, we report the synthesis and characterization of the dilanthanide compounds [(CpiPr5Ln)2(μ-η6:η6-C6H6)][Fe(N(SiMe3)2)3] (Ln = Y, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm; CpiPr5 = pentaisopropylcyclopentadienyl), featuring cationic inverse sandwich complexes in which two Ln centers are bridged by a planar benzene trianion radical. These compounds are synthesized via one-electron oxidation of (CpiPr5Ln)2(μ-η6:η6-C6H6) using Fe(N(SiMe3)2)3 as a mild outer-sphere oxidant. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals inverse sandwich structures featuring a planar benzene bridge and structural signatures of extended δ-bonding along the Cp–Ln–Bz–Ln–Cp axis. Continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy of the congener containing diamagnetic Y3+ supports assignment of an S = 1/2 benzene trianion radical. Magnetometry measurements on the Gd analogue reveal the presence of remarkably strong ferromagnetic coupling (J = +55.6(6) cm–1) between the S = 7/2 Gd3+ centers and the benzene radical, giving rise to a well-isolated S = 15/2 ground state. These observations are explained through a molecular orbital analysis, which indicates that the δ-symmetric (CpiPr5)− ligands lower the energy of the Ln3+ dδ (dxy and dx2–y2) orbitals. Importantly, this electronic structure facilitates enhanced covalency with the benzene trianion radical, leading to greater than 30% metal character in the radical-based singly occupied molecular orbital (SOMO). The results establish a new regime of radical-mediated lanthanide exchange coupling in which substantial ground-state metal character within the radical SOMO drives strong intraatomic-like ferromagnetic exchange akin to Hund’s first rule.

doi:10.1063/5.0337390.title: Design optimization of flux concentrators for magnetic tunnel junctions-based sensors
doi:10.1063/5.0337390.abstract: Miniaturized, ultra-sensitive, and easily integrable magnetometers are needed for many applications, such as space exploration or health monitoring. Achieving this goal requires a magnetic sensor with high sensitivity and low noise. High sensitivity (>1000%/mT) can be obtained by integrating high gain Permalloy flux concentrators (FC), with the advantage of high field direction selectivity. Reducing the magnetic 1/f noise can be realized by increasing the number of magnetic tunnel junctions in the air-gap of the FC. However, this is obtained at the expense of a larger air-gap and consequently a decrease in the magnetic gain and thus in the sensitivity. In this paper, we explore a design optimization scheme in order to find the best trade-off between high FC gain and low magnetic noise. To model the gain of the flux concentrator, we propose two complementary approaches; one is based on finite-element simulations of the FC gain, where the influence of geometrical parameters of the air-gap is investigated. Then, in a second step, we propose an analytical formula consistent with all our simulation results and based on magnetic reluctance. Finally, we derive an analytical model of the sensor detectivity from which we can extract the optimal sensor design, which allows an improvement by three orders of magnitude in the performance compared to a single junction. Our research demonstrates that a multi-parameter approach outperforms single-parameter optimization, with peak performance surprisingly achieved at moderate parameter values.

doi:10.1063/5.0350854.title: Controlling carrier localization in 2D lead-free halide perovskites for dual-functional photodetector and photosynapse
doi:10.1063/5.0350854.abstract: Low-dimensional tin halide perovskites are regarded as ideal channel materials for phototransistors owing to their high carrier mobility and light absorption coefficient. To date, phototransistors have been developed along two distinct directions: photodetectors with rapid response and recovery dynamics, and photosynapses with persistent photoconductivity and slow decay characteristics for emulating long-term memory. However, strategies to simultaneously achieve these divergent functionalities remain poorly understood. In this work, the defect density and carrier dynamics in PEA2SnI4 films are tuned through a solvent engineering approach, enabling dual operational modes for photodetector and photosynapse devices. Phototransistors based on dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) exhibit defect-assisted carrier localization, leading to robust synaptic behavior. In comparison, 1,3-dimethyl-2-imidazolidinone (DMI) suppresses trapping sites, enabling fast photoresponse for photodetection. This work provides insights into the defect-mediated photoresponse mechanisms and offers a rationale for tailoring tin perovskite phototransistors in multifunctional optoelectronics.

doi:10.1063/5.0349993.title: On the origin of nonreciprocal charge transport in topological insulator BiSbTeSe2
doi:10.1063/5.0349993.abstract: Nonreciprocal charge transport provides an effective approach for probing direction-dependent charge dynamics and spin-momentum-locked electronic states. Here, we report highly gate-tunable nonreciprocal charge transport in a dual-gated BiSbTeSe2 topological insulator device. The second-harmonic longitudinal resistance is linear in both current and magnetic field. The nonreciprocal response reaches its maximum near the charge neutrality point, exhibits sign reversals on either side, and is strongly suppressed once the Fermi level enters the bulk states. We suggest that the nonreciprocal response is attributed to the inhomogeneity of spin-momentum locking in the topological surface states. The nonreciprocal signal near the charge neutrality point is about one order of magnitude larger than that without gate modulation and remains robust up to 300 K, highlighting BiSbTeSe2 as a promising platform for room-temperature nonlinear electronics.

doi:10.1063/5.0353242.title: Hybridization of a magnon mode with a higher-order topological photonic corner state
doi:10.1063/5.0353242.abstract: Photonic corner states in higher-order topological lattices combine topological localization with zero-dimensional field confinement, making them promising interfaces for enhanced light–matter interactions. Yet their coupling to material excitations remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate hybridization between the Kittel mode of a yttrium iron garnet sphere and a higher-order topological photonic corner state in a two-dimensional Su–Schrieffer–Heeger microwave lattice. Tuning the Kittel mode through the corner-state resonance produces a pronounced avoided crossing with a minimum frequency splitting of 155.44 MHz. Moving the same sphere to the adjacent site reduces the splitting to 36.22 MHz, whereas no splitting is resolved in the bulk. The resulting coupling-strength map is concentrated at the corners and corroborates the corner-state assignment relative to extended edge and bulk modes. Our results show that higher-order topological corner states can serve as localized interfaces for cavity magnonics and hybrid topological light–matter systems.

doi:10.1002/adfm.79104.title: Suppression and Reemergence of Directional Transport across the Ferromagnetic Transition in SrRuO 3
doi:10.1002/adfm.79104.abstract: ABSTRACT SrRuO 3 is a canonical itinerant ferromagnet that continues to serve as a fertile platform for exploring spin‐orbit coupled transport and topological responses in correlated oxide metals. Here, we investigate a (110)‐oriented epitaxial SrRuO 3 thin film on DyScO 3 , where crystallographic anisotropy allows for symmetry‐resolved charge transport along orthogonal in‐plane directions. We uncover two principal findings. First, the resistance above the Curie temperature T c ,on ≈ 165 K exhibits strong anisotropy, consistent with directionally dependent spin‐fluctuation scattering. Below T c ,on , this anisotropy nearly vanishes, despite persistent structural inequivalence, due to isotropic electron‐magnon and electron‐electron scattering processes. Second, the application of a magnetic field reveals a striking directional contrast in the linear magnetoresistance ( MR ): it remains negative and saturates along [001], but changes sign and becomes positive along below T 0 = 145 K. In contrast, the quadratic MR term is identical for both directions and peaks near , where the ordinary Hall coefficient crosses zero, consistent with carrier compensation under a two‐band scenario. A sign change in the anomalous Hall signal at is consistent with a temperature‐dependent redistribution of Berry‐curvature contributions near the Fermi level. These results establish ferromagnetic ordering as the primary driver of the observed directional magnetotransport in SrRuO 3 .

doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c10331.title: Unfolding of Field-Free Spin–Orbit Torque Magnetization Switching in a van der Waals Heterostructure
doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c10331.abstract: Abstract Heterostructures of 2D materials offer high tunability of magnetic properties, including current-induced magnetization switching by unconventional spin–orbit torques. The microscopic mechanisms governing spin-torque switching in van der Waals systems, however, remain insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate current-induced magnetization reversal in an Fe3GeTe2 (FGT) and WTe2 heterostructure using scanning harmonic magneto-optical Kerr effect microscopy. Spatially resolved magnetization maps show that field-free switching unfolds from asymmetric domain nucleation at the edges of the FGT flake, followed by domain wall propagation. This switching behavior is deterministic and bipolar, consistent with spin–orbit torques arising from the injection of both in-plane and out-of-plane spins from WTe2 into FGT. The critical currents for up-to-down and down-to-up switching differ because of asymmetric domain nucleation and directional domain wall pinning effects. Micromagnetic simulations reproduce the switching behavior observed experimentally, showing how the initial domain nucleation sites are determined by the sample geometry and combined influence of in-plane and out-of-plane spins and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Finally, by systematically varying the field-like and damping-like torque components and sweeping the spin polarization between in-plane and out-of-plane, we identify the torque configurations that yield the most efficient switching in van der Waals magnets with different shapes.

doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c14517.title: Ferroelectric Switching of Skyrmion Topology in 2D Multiferroics
doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c14517.abstract: Abstract Deterministic switching of skyrmion topology is a central frontier in topological spintronics, yet current paradigms rely almost exclusively on dissipative-current-driven spin torques. Here, we propose a fundamentally distinct mechanism for the nonvolatile switching of the skyrmion topology in two-dimensional multiferroics. We reveal that the intrinsic magnetoelectric coupling intimately links the out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization to interlayer magnetic exchange. Consequently, an electric-field-driven polarization reversal deterministically converts the interlayer coupling between the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states. This macroscopic exchange reversal directly flips the microscopic skyrmion core polarity and reverses its topological charge, thereby stabilizing the two electrically addressable topological phases. Guided by our established design principles, we rigorously validate this mechanism in a Co2CF2/MoN2 multiferroic heterostructure by using combined first-principles calculations and atomistic spin simulations. Our findings bypass the limitations of continuous current injection, establishing a robust physical framework for energy-efficient multiferroic topological spintronics.

doi:10.1021/acsaelm.6c01591.title: Strain-Engineered Giant Tunneling Magnetoresistance in Fe-Intercalated MoS2 van der Waals Magnetic Tunnel Junctions
doi:10.1021/acsaelm.6c01591.abstract: Abstract This work proposes an all-two-dimensional magnetic tunnel junction consisting of Fe-intercalated MoS2 ferromagnetic electrodes and a pristine bilayer MoS2 tunneling barrier. We systematically investigate the modulation mechanism of out-of-plane tensile strain on the spin-transport properties of the device using quantum transport simulations. The results reveal that Fe intercalation induces a semiconductor-to-ferromagnetic-metal transition in MoS2 and the magnetic moment increases progressively under tensile strain. Under an applied tensile strain of 3%, the MTJ achieves an ultrahigh tunneling magnetoresistance of 1.67 × 105% accompanied by a spin injection efficiency of 90%. The enhancement of spin-dependent tunneling efficiency under tensile strain originates from a Fermi level shift of the electrodes and modulation of the spin asymmetry of the interfacial Schottky barrier. By integrating atomic intercalation with strain engineering, this work establishes a new paradigm for designing high-performance, low-power two-dimensional spintronic devices.

doi:10.1016/j.jmmm.2026.174697.title: Magnetic tunnel junctions: the evolution, impact and perspective
doi:10.1016/j.jmmm.2026.174697.journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials
doi:10.1016/j.jmmm.2026.174697.abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) study in the past three decades, resulting in over 25,000 publications while adding 1000 more each year, has become among the most persuasive areas of research. MTJ devices lead the ubiquitous success of spintronics for technological advancement from most aspects of information technology to health sciences, with unprecedented, all-encompassing benefits to the society. We navigate through the evolution of the developing field of MTJs and the related technologies, with continued efforts for improving the tunnel magnetoresistance ratio. The MTJs' excellent ability to convert spin signals to charge signals secures their extensive commercial applications in magnetic data storage and field sensing. More advanced implementation and progress such as with neuromorphic and probabilistic computing entail from here.

doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03208.title: Ultrafast Mimic of Spin Hall Effect in Altermagnets
doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03208.abstract: Abstract The spin Hall effect, a key effect in creating spin currents and controlling magnetic order at the nanoscale, presupposes a population of mobile carriers in a conducting state, in which a driving charge current generates a perpendicular spin-current. Here we show an ultrafast light-wave driven spin Hall analogue exists in altermagnetic semiconductors and insulators, in which a laser pulse generates both a charge current and a co-occurring perpendicular pure spin current. Employing the example of the theoretically predicted 2d altermagnetic Lieb-lattice semiconductor Cr2SO, we demonstrate that pulse design allows lightwave control over the postpulse spin/charge current ratio ξres, with values exceeding unity obtained in the multicycle regime. Our findings thus both considerably broaden the materials base for spin Hall/spin splitter physics, as well as establishing 2d altermagnets as a platform providing a new route for valleytronic lightwave control of spin- and charge currents at ultrafast times.

doi:10.1002/adma.75391.title: Optically Tunable Chiral Magnetic States and Exchange Engineering via Charge‐Transfer Excitation in a van der Waals Antiferromagnet CrPS 4
doi:10.1002/adma.75391.abstract: ABSTRACT Controlling magnetism with light in two‐dimensional van der Waals magnets could enable ultrafast, energy‐efficient spintronics. However, selectively writing distinct magnetic phases, such as chiral magnetic states (e.g., spin spirals and skyrmions) for memory and collinear states for logic, within a single material remains an outstanding challenge. Here, we demonstrate deterministic, photon‐energy‐selective writing of magnetic order in the air‐stable antiferromagnet chromium thiophosphate (). Its ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer gap serves as an intrinsic switching threshold: excitation below this gap drives – transitions to stabilize chiral magnetic states due to a spin–spiral phase, while excitation above activates a photo‐doping mechanism that renormalizes magnetic exchange and induces a collinear phase. These optically defined states are distinguished through polarization‐resolved magneto‐optical spectroscopy and probed via a proximal monolayer tungsten diselenide (). By establishing optical selectivity in a single material, our work provides a reconfigurable platform for opto‐spintronic circuits where memory and logic functions can be dynamically toggled with light.
